paper_title: Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence. In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly. Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer. Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves. To strengthen this capability, we propose EvidenceConnect, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence. To ensure quality, a reference answer is retained only when independent VLMs agree on it, and region-ablation tests discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions. We then train base VLMs on the resulting data with RLVR, obtaining Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2). Although the synthesized data are not tailored to any downstream benchmark, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with further gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning. These results establish EvidenceConnect as an effective framework for supervising evidence connection and suggest that strengthening this shared capability leads to more generalizable multimodal perception.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Multimodal perception is the foundation of multimodal intelligence: before multimodal model can reason or act, it must determine what is present in scene. Recent progress on this front, such as multimodal Chain-of-Thought (Zhang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024; Li & Ma, 2026) and Thinkingwith-Images (Zheng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025c), has improved the ability of open-source vision-language models (VLMs) to perceive fine-grained visual content and use it in reasoning (Wei et al., 2026; 2025b; Li et al., 2026b). However, these advances do not reliably extend to tasks in which critical visual cues are dispersed across objects, relationships, frames, or dialogue turns. Two such tasks, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding, are particularly important because they underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents, respectively. Spatial perception requires model to recover how entities are arranged relative to one another and how several spatial relations compose (Gemini Robotics Team, 2025; Li et al., 2025a). Embodied AI relies on it to ground navigation, manipulation, and viewpoint-dependent decisions in object locations and spatial relations (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026). Multimodal long-context understanding requires model to locate evidence across images and dialogue history, preserve entity identity, and bring that evidence to bear on the current question (Wu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025d; Song et al., 2024). Multimodal agents rely on it to retrieve relevant past observations, resolve references across interactions, and integrate earlier evidence into current decisions (He et al., 2024; Su et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025b). Strengthening these capabilities, however, is constrained by the difficulty of building high-quality training data. For spatial perception, existing efforts mainly scale up region-grounded relational data (Chen et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2026a), but reliable labels require precise localization and relational grounding across multiple objects. Such labels are expensive to annotate by hand, while automated generators often hallucinate relations. For long-context understanding, existing multiimage and multi-turn instruction data (Jiang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024) concentrate on few formats and task types, because diverse questions that remain answerable over long sequences are hard to construct automatically. Data for embodied spatial reasoning and multimodal agents are even harder to synthesize, since they additionally involve physical or interactive environments and multi-step trajectories. Consequently, neither these capabilities nor the applications built on them have scalable and high-quality source of clean, verifiable supervision. Our key insight is that these tasks build on shared atomic capability of VLMs, which we call connecting evidence: identifying task-relevant visual facts, binding each fact to the correct entity, recovering the relations among them, and integrating the evidence into an answer. These tasks instantiate this capability differently: spatial perception connects objects within scene through spatial relations, whereas long-context understanding, on which multimodal agents rely, connects facts across images and dialogue turns through entity identity and reference. Despite these differences in where the evidence resides and how it is linked, both tasks rely on the same underlying steps, so strengthening these steps can benefit both. Moreover, since the first step, identifying visual facts, is itself fine-grained perception, fine-grained perception benefits as well. Crucially, training data that target this capability are far easier to construct and verify than data for the tasks themselves. To turn this insight into trainable supervision, we propose EVIDENCECONNECT, an easy-to-implement, fully automated framework that synthesizes visual questions requiring the model to connect evidence across regions. Specifically, we select group of related regions within single image and synthesize compositional question over them from privileged zoomed views, which make small details visible but are used only during data construction. Depending on

Answering such questions thus exercises the same steps as the target tasks: relating regions spatially, including from given viewpoint, parallels spatial perception and embodied spatial reasoning, whereas locating scattered regions, binding their facts to the right references, and integrating them parallels long-context understanding and multimodal agents. To ensure data quality, we keep question only if VLMs from different families agree on its answer, and we use region-ablation tests to discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions. Finally, each verified question is converted into multiple-choice form for rule-based rewards and paired with the full image, where colored outlines typically mark the selected regions to avoid ambiguous references, so the model must still perceive and connect the evidence by itself. To evaluate whether this supervision generalizes beyond the synthesized questions, we train Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B, and Qwen3.6-27B (Qwen Team, 2026a;b) with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Lambert et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2025) using only our synthesized data, without supervised fine-tuning or benchmark-specific question formats. The resulting models, ZwZ2-4B/9B/27B, achieve substantial improvements in fine-grained and spatial perception as well as multimodal long-context understanding, with gains that further extend to embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning. For example, ZwZ2-4B improves over its base model from 37.43 to 45.26 (+7.83) on ViewSpatial-Bench (spatial reasoning) and from 60.08 to 70.08 (+10.00) on MileBench (long-context understanding). More broadly, its average over all 25 benchmarks increases from 49.41 to 54.79, and the corresponding averages improve from 51.63 to 56.59 for ZwZ2-9B and from 55.52 to 60.51 for ZwZ2-27B. Notably, although ZwZ2 is trained only on single images, it also improves on multi-image long-context benchmarks and multimodal agent tasks. These results demonstrate that connecting evidence is indeed generalizable training target for multimodal perception. To summarize, our key contributions are the following: We identify connecting evidence as an important atomic capability of VLMs, underlying finegrained perception, spatial perception, and multimodal long-context understanding. We develop EVIDENCECONNECT, structured and audited synthesis pipeline for single-image, multi-region compositional questions, with privileged region views and independent checks for answer correctness and evidence dependence. Experiments demonstrate that RLVR on the resulting synthetic data improves broad range of perception benchmarks and further generalizes to many real-world tasks, including embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Spatial perception. Spatial perception underpins embodied tasks such as robotic manipulation and embodied question answering (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025; Gemini Robotics Team, 2025). Existing approaches use large-scale spatial supervision (Chen et al., 2024a), intermediate visual grounding (Zhang et al., 2026a), and progressive training (Li et al., 2026a). Benchmarks and associated training resources examine perspective-taking, multi-image inference, and multi-hop composition (Li et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2026). MultihopSpatial additionally studies grounded spatial training and its transfer to embodied tasks (Lee et al., 2026). Euclids Gift (Lian et al., 2026) demonstrates transfer from geometric surrogate tasks. Similarly, we train on surrogate task and evaluate its transfer, but our task is built from natural images and targets the evidence connection shared by spatial perception and long-context understanding, rather than spatial skills alone. Long-context multimodal understanding. Multimodal long-context understanding requires locating, tracking, and integrating evidence across long sequences of images and dialogue turns. Existing efforts support these abilities through multi-image and multi-turn instruction tuning (Jiang et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024) and dialogue-fragment retrieval (Bi et al., 2026), while benchmarks assess long-context integration and memory (Song et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025d; Ren et al., 2026). Controlled studies nevertheless identify persistent difficulties in aggregating distributed visual information (Das et al., 2026). We target evidence connection as shared component of these tasks, constructing single-image questions that require identifying, binding, and composing facts across regions. Multimodal synthetic data. Early resources provide annotated scene graphs and programmatic questions (Krishna et al., 2017; Hudson & Manning, 2019). Later methods automate instruction generation (Zhao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), evolution (Luo et al., 2025), and synthesis for unsupervised post-training (Wei et al., 2025a). Zooming without Zooming (Wei et al., 2026) transfers single-region supervision to full images with cross-model answer checks. CRIT (Sung et al., 2026) and FM2DS (Abaskohi et al., 2024) synthesize cross-modal questions and filter unimodal shortcuts, while MM-CondChain (Shen et al., 2026) verifies conditional programs and ReasonVQA (Tran et al., 2025) composes external knowledge paths. HopChain (Wang et al., 2026) targets long-CoT robustness through instance-dependent chains with human-verified answers. Unlike these pipelines, EVIDENCECONNECT builds each question on coherent group of regions rather than single region or sequential chain, so its questions cover aggregation and closed-set comparison in addition to dependency chains. Moreover, it automatically checks both the answer and its dependence on the selected regions, through cross-model agreement and region ablation, without human annotation.

sections.title: VISUAL EVIDENCE
sections.content: As discussed in Section 1, fine-grained perception, spatial perception, and multimodal long-context understanding share core capability that we call connecting evidence. This motivates training data whose questions structurally require this capability and end in concise answers suitable for verifiable rewards. To construct this supervision, we propose EVIDENCECONNECT, data synthesis framework centered on coherent groups of image regions. Within this framework, high-resolution privileged crops render local details visible for question synthesis, while cross-model answer anchoring and region ablation check label reliability and evidence dependence. The overview of the data synthesis pipeline is shown in Figure 2. 3.1 MULTI-REGION QUESTION SYNTHESIS Target question structure. We first define the target question, whose answer depends on connecting one coherent group of regions in an image. Formally, from source image I, we obtain

Restricting the evidence to single image keeps training inexpensive, while several related regions of one image already require model to locate, bind, and compose dispersed evidence. Importantly, the regions are selected to jointly support one question q, which assigns each of them role, i.e., the fact it contributes: value to be combined, member of closed candidate set, or clue on which later step depends. Corresponding to these three kinds of roles, connects the regions through one of three forms. Aggregation combines counts or other numeric facts from the regions, possibly through short calculation. Comparison and matching treats the regions as the complete candidate set, so that an answer such as an outlier, an extremum, or pairing can be identified only by considering all of them. Dependency chains and compositions build the answer in several steps, e.g., by using clue to decide what to read next, fixing viewpoint for interpreting the rest, or combining predicates from different regions. In all three forms, the answer is determined only when the assigned roles are taken together. These forms also tie our questions to the target tasks: spatial relations, including those in an agents or objects own frame, parallel spatial perception and embodied spatial reasoning, while binding facts to regions referenced by outline colors and integrating them parallels how long-context understanding and multimodal agents handle facts tied to image or turn references. To synthesize such questions, we first locate candidate regions, then group those that support one of the three forms, and finally compose questions over each selected group. Grounded evidence discovery. Since multi-region questions need detail-rich scenes, we start from high-resolution, visually complex images. For each image, strong VLM judges whether it can support such questions and, if so, is prompted to propose concrete, clearly localizable regions, each with bounding box and short description, prioritizing regions that can be related to one another over isolated salient ones. We then discard proposals that are too small, too large, or heavily overlapping. As these model-generated descriptions may be wrong, they only guide grouping and question writing, whereas reference answers are later derived from the image itself. Task-conditioned evidence grouping. An arbitrary collection of these proposals, however, does not necessarily support valid compositional question. We therefore prompt strong model with the image caption and region descriptions to propose several groups per image, each labeled with task family (a specific question type such as anomaly detection) and necessity mode (how removing region should affect the answer). We then discard invalid or duplicated groups and closed sets of incomparable objects, and keep groups with distinct task families first. The task family only guides question writing, whereas each regions concrete role is fixed when question is written. Privileged evidence layout. Since fine-grained details are difficult to inspect at full-image scale, we construct for each group privileged evidence layout VG, which is accessible only during data construction. Following the layout-preserving design of Liu et al. (2025), VG arranges nativeresolution crops of the selected regions, with small context margins, on compact canvas that removes irrelevant background while preserving their relative horizontal and vertical order. In addition, each region is outlined in distinct color that also marks it in the full image, allowing questions to refer to regions by color unambiguously. Finally, VG serves as the sole visual input to the question generator, which confines its questions to evidence within the group, and it is later reused for verification (Section 3.2). Question realization. The question generator, strong VLM, then receives VG, the region descriptions, and few reasoning blueprints, i.e., templates of reasoning programs, and composes several candidate questions, each with concise answer: single value (e.g., number, short phrase, or the outline color of selected region), set, or an ordered pair. To make its use of evidence checkable, the generator also states each regions contribution and the answer expected after removing it, together with reasoning certificate, i.e., short sequence of steps that links the regions to the answer. Deterministic rules then reject candidates whose certificate leaves region unused or contains steps that do not lead to the answer, whose own predicted answer survives the removal of region, or that use subjective wording, leak the answer through an outline color, or contain inconsistent arithmetic. Implementation details and prompt templates appear in Appendices and B.

Adaptive drop-one testing. Agreement on a, however, does not show that the answer actually depends on the selected evidence. Since every question is constructed to require all of its regions (Section 3.1), an answer that survives the removal of region indicates defect, such as decorative region or shortcut that bypasses the intended reasoning. To detect such defects, we mask each ri in the privileged layout, = Mi(VG), where Mi replaces the crop of ri with gray placeholder. verifier from one anchoring family then answers from this view, reporting insufficient information if the masked evidence is needed, and either such report or changed answer confirms that the question depends on ri. If instead is still returned, or the response is unusable, we query the verifier again and mark ri as empirically redundant only if most queries recover a. Note that single redundant region, however, may reflect noise rather than defect, because part of masked region can remain visible in an adjacent crop through overlapping context margins, and individual responses also vary. We therefore reject question only when more than one region is redundant, which also improves synthesis efficiency, since stricter rule would discard many potentially valid questions merely because one region was judged redundant. Since the policy, i.e., the model under training, never sees VG, each verified candidate is paired with policy view VI , by default the source image with each selected region outlined in its assigned color. To avoid ambiguous references in the full image, these outlines mark which instances question refers to, without revealing the answer-bearing content that the policy must still perceive and compose. For aggregate questions, whose answers do not depend on the outlines, we also try to replace marker references with natural descriptions, so that the policy must locate the evidence itself. This unmarked version replaces the marked one only if independent audits by both anchoring families, without access to a, confirm unique references, an unchanged multi-region task grounded in the intended regions, and the answer a. Multiple-choice conversion and difficulty filtering. To support rule-based rewards in RLVR, we then turn each question into four-option multiple-choice question, adding three distractors in the answer format of so that the format does not reveal the answer. Finally, since overly easy examples provide little learning signal, lightweight VLM answers each example several times, and we discard examples that it always answers correctly.

In particular, fine-grained and spatial perception improve by 5.26.3 points on average, with gains of up to 11.1 points on MIMIC and 10.8 points on CountQA, and embodied spatial reasoning improves by 5.58.1 points, including 10.5 points on ERQA at 27B. Qualitative examples are provided in Appendix F. Notably, although ZwZ2 is trained only on single images, its gains carry over to multi-image and interactive settings. Long-context understanding improves at every scale, most markedly at 4B, where the domain average rises by 5.6 points, including gain of 10.0 points on MileBench. Likewise, the multimodal agent benchmark AgentVista improves by 4.86.2 points, and GUI grounding also improves consistently. These results support our premise that connecting evidence within an image transfers to tasks whose evidence spans images, dialogue turns, or interaction steps. ZwZ2 remains competitive with frontier models. ZwZ2-27B achieves the highest overall accuracy (60.51%), compared with 54.02%, 57.24%, and 55.47% for GPT-5.6-Luna, GLM-5.3-Flash, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, and leads the fine-grained perception domain. 4.3 COMPARISON WITH EXISTING TRAINING DATA Table 2 compares EVIDENCECONNECT with existing synthetic datasets on the same 4B base model. These datasets target single-region fine-grained perception (ZwZ), grounded counting and spatial reasoning (TVG), dialogue-fragment retrieval (F2RVLM), cross-modal multi-hop QA over interleaved contexts (CRIT), and knowledge-based multi-hop QA (MMHops). Training on TVG, F2RVLM, CRIT, or MMHops improves MileBench but degrades HR-Bench, CountQA, MindCubeTiny, and MemLens, and all four datasets lower the average accuracy below that of the base model. In contrast, EVIDENCECONNECT improves every benchmark over the base model and outperforms these four datasets on all 11 benchmarks, with comparable amount of data (20.4K examples versus 19.4K37K). ZwZ-73K is the strongest baseline. Since it also synthesizes questions from zoomed-in views but grounds each question in single region, the comparison with ZwZ serves as an approximate ablation of connecting multiple regions. Although ZwZ uses 3.6 as many examples (73K versus 20.4K), EVIDENCECONNECT raises the average accuracy from 49.86 to 53.86 and surpasses ZwZ on 10 of the 11 benchmarks, trailing it only on MileBench by 0.13 points. The largest margin appears on MindCube-Tiny, where ZwZ reduces accuracy by 13.8 points whereas EVIDENCECONNECT improves it by 5.4 points. This contrast is consistent with our premise that embodied spatial reasoning relies on connecting evidence across regions rather than on inspecting single region.

sections.title: 4.4 ABLATION STUDIES
sections.content: Ablation study on drop-one verification. To evaluate adaptive drop-one verification during data synthesis, we compare Qwen3.5-4B trained on 7K examples constructed with or without this verification step  (Table 3)  . As described in Section 3.2, this step masks one selected region at time in the privileged layout and tests whether the reference answer remains recoverable. When the verifier returns the reference answer or an unusable response, additional queries are used; region is marked as empirically redundant only if most queries recover the reference answer. question is rejected only when more than one region is empirically redundant, allowing for noise from overlapping crop margins and variable verifier responses. With drop-one verification, average accuracy rises from 51.03 to 52.65 (+1.63 points), with improvements on 10 of the 11 benchmarks. The largest gains are on MindCube-Tiny (+5.15), O3-Bench (+4.64), and CountQA (+3.79), while ERQA decreases by 4.00 points. These results support the usefulness of this synthesis-time verification step for downstream performance, although its gains are not uniform across tasks. Ablation study on privileged views. To examine the role of privileged views, we train Qwen3.54B on 7K examples synthesized from privileged views or original images, with all other settings fixed  (Table 3)  . Synthesis from privileged views achieves higher average accuracy than synthesis from original images (52.65 versus 51.38), with higher scores on 9 of the 11 benchmarks. Originalimage synthesis performs better on Chartography and ERQA, by 4.00 and 4.75 points, respectively. Thus, privileged-view synthesis improves average accuracy by 1.27 points in this 7K comparison, although its gains are not uniform across benchmarks. 4.5 ANALYSIS Generalization to Qwen3-VL. To examine whether the gains extend beyond the base models used in the experiments, we evaluate Qwen3VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B before and after training on the same 11 benchmarks in Table 2. Figure 3 reports average scores of 36.82 and 41.63 for Qwen3-VL-2B, and 41.70 and 44.61 for Qwen3-VL-4B, corresponding to gains of 4.81 and 2.91 points, respectively. These results suggest that the benefits of supervision extend to additional base models at both scales. Figure 3: Qwen3-VL generalization. Figure 4: Effect of training data scale. Effect of training data scale. Figure 4 compares Qwen3.5-4B at different training data scales on the same 11 benchmarks. Average accuracy over the 11 benchmarks in Table 2 increases from 47.16 for the base model to 52.65 with 7K training examples and 53.86 with the full 20.4K training set. The full set yields further improvement of 1.21 points over 7K examples, while the 7K setting already improves over the base model by 5.49 points. Context length. Figure 5 breaks down MemLens and the MMLongBench visual core by context length. ZwZ2 outperforms or matches its base model at every length and scale, and on MemLens its gains persist up to 256K tokens. The gains, however, narrow at the longest contexts. At 128K on the MMLongBench visual core, for example, ZwZ2-4B and ZwZ2-9B merely match their base models.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented EVIDENCECONNECT, fully automated framework that synthesizes multi-region visual questions and answers, requiring model to connect evidence within an image. Trained with RLVR on these data alone, ZwZ2 improves over its base models on all 25 benchmarks at 4B, 9B, and 27B. Notably, although training uses only single images, the gains extend beyond fine-grained and spatial perception to embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, and multimodal agent tasks. These results suggest that connecting evidence is transferable training target, and thus tasks whose training data are costly to build can benefit from data that are far easier to construct and verify.

Before any model call, we keep only images whose longer side has at least 1280 pixels, whose mean per-channel intensity entropy is at least 6.5 bits, whose Canny edge density is at least 0.04, and whose luminance standard deviation is at least 60. Grounded evidence discovery. For each image, single call with the image and its caption (Prompt B.1) judges whether the image can support multi-region questions and returns up to 18 region proposals, whose box coordinates are converted to pixels and clamped to the image. We then discard boxes that cover less than 0.04% or more than 18% of the image, as well as boxes whose IoU with an earlier kept box is at least 0.65. Images judged unsuitable, or with fewer than four remaining regions, are skipped. sections.title: C TRAINING DATA STATISTICS
sections.content: Our training set contains 20.4K examples synthesized from SA-1B images by the pipeline in Section 3 and Appendix A, and Figure 7 summarizes its composition. Each example involves three to seven regions, most often three (65.74%) or four (24.34%), followed by five (7.93%) and six or seven (1.99%). The difficulty levels, defined by how many of the four screening responses are correct, are broadly distributed. Specifically, easy, medium, hard, and very hard examples account for 33.75%, 22.04%, 19.07%, and 25.14% of the data, so more than 44% of the examples are hard or very hard. Very hard examples, which the screening model never answers correctly, are kept, since their reference answers have already been anchored by two stronger VLMs.

sections.title: D TRAINING DETAILS
sections.content: All models are trained with the same GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) configuration for two epochs, with batch size of 128 and learning rate of 106. For each prompt, we sample G=8 rollouts at temperature 0.7 with maximum response length of 32K tokens, and the thinking mode is disabled during rollouts to keep responses concise. We use decoupled clipping ratios ϵlow=0.2 and ϵhigh=0.3, as proposed in DAPO (Yu et al., 2025), and remove the KL penalty (βKL=0), so that the policy is not anchored to the base model. Finally, the reward checks whether the predicted option letter matches the ground-truth option.

sections.title: F CASE STUDY
sections.content: To complement the quantitative evaluation, we examine three selected examples in which ZwZ24B answers correctly while its base model, Qwen3.5-4B, fails. Figure 8 presents examples from MIMIC, ZoomBench, and CountQA, covering cross-image category identification, spatially specified text recognition, and object counting. We analyze the models visible responses to identify how their answers differ in the use of visual evidence and the satisfaction of question constraints. Cross-image consistency. In Figure 8(a), the MIMIC question asks for category that appears in all five images. The base model selects wine glass, even though its response explicitly acknowledges that this object is absent from some images. It justifies the answer by referring to the most prominent shared item across the majority of the set, effectively replacing the requirement of universal presence with majority overlap. ZwZ2 checks candidate categories against the full set of images. Its response rules out wine glass because it is absent from Images 4 and 5, and identifies person as the category shared by all five images. This example illustrates the importance of preserving the questions scope when integrating evidence across images: an object shared by several images does not necessarily satisfy constraint over the entire set. Question-conditioned text localization. Figure 8(b) asks for the black text above the lower archway. The base model recognizes the word SEGATORI on the adjacent building, but associates the question with inscriptions on the fountain and ultimately selects FONTE. Its response therefore reveals mismatch between the recognized text and the region specified by the question. ZwZ2 identifies the entrance of the yellow building as the relevant lower archway and reads the sign immediately above it, yielding the correct answer, SEGATORI. The case highlights the role of spatial reference resolution in visual text understanding: recognizing visible word must be accompanied by establishing whether it belongs to the queried location. sections.title: G LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: Our work has two main limitations. First, although our single-image supervision transfers to multiimage and agent tasks, it does not directly model temporal or cross-frame dependencies, so extending the synthesis to evidence spread across video frames is natural next step. Second, we apply RLVR to models of up to 27B parameters, and whether the same supervision benefits larger models or earlier training stages, such as pre-training, remains to be studied.
